Neonates of the Desert Skink (Liopholis inornata) emerge from parchment-shelled eggs with a total length of 4.2 cm [Lb = 4.2 cm], a modest size that reflects the constraints of the arid zone environment where yolk reserves must support full development. The wet weight at birth is 1.85 g [Wwb = 1.85 g], a value consistent with the limited maternal provisioning observed in small scincid lizards. Gestation and the incubation period appear to be intricately tied to thermal conditions; females collected in the field and brought into the laboratory gave birth after approximately 120 days [ab = approximately 120 days] at a constant temperature of 26.571 °C [T = 26.571 °C]. This relatively extended period underscores the species' reliance on seasonal temperature cues for successful embryogenesis. The yolk-sac larva transitions to first exogenous feeding within days of emergence, a critical trophic switch that initiates a phase of rapid mass gain. Juveniles exhibit a growth trajectory that is initially steep but decelerates markedly as they approach the threshold of gonadal maturation.

Under the thermal regime approximating active field conditions at 23.67075 °C [T = 23.67075 °C], the maximum reproductive output achievable by a female Desert Skink can be described by a clutch frequency of up to two clutches per year [F_R_i = up to two clutches per year], each containing 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch]. This annual reproductive schedule is relatively modest, typical of a K-selected squamate inhabiting unpredictable, resource-poor environments. The reproductive activation that triggers the first egg clutch occurs approximately 446 days after birth, based on the mean time required to reach 6 cm in total length under captive conditions at 26.571 °C [T = 26.571 °C], yielding an age at first reproduction of 446 days after birth [tR = 446 days after birth]. This delayed onset of breeding suggests that females require multiple growing seasons to accumulate sufficient body condition to support vitellogenesis and gestation, a pattern common among small terrestrial reptiles from temperate zones.

Body size at the onset of reproductive activity in the Desert Skink is defined by the total length at puberty, which field records place at 6.0 cm [Lp = 6.0 cm], a value corroborated by the smallest gravid female captured during surveys, which measured 6.4 cm. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from the species-specific length-weight relationship, is approximately 7.63 g [Wwp = approximately 7.63 g], a mass that represents a substantial energetic investment over the 1.85 g neonatal state. This tripling of body mass prior to first reproduction reflects the accumulation of skeletal material and visceral fat reserves necessary to sustain gestation. The ultimate total length attained by adults is 8.6 cm [Li = 8.6 cm], a ceiling beyond which further somatic growth is negligible. Using the same allometric relationship, the ultimate wet weight at this maximal size is around 21.41 g [Wwi = around 21.41 g]. This asymptotic mass is consistent with the maximum body size observed in museum series and field samples, indicating that individuals approach this plateau within a few years of reaching sexual maturity.

Longevity records for the Desert Skink are sparse, but available data suggest that members of the genus Liopholis may live for up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years] at typical field temperatures of 23.67075 °C [T = 23.67075 °C]. This extended lifespan is relatively unusual for a skink of this body size and points to a low-mortality, slow-paced life history strategy adapted to the harsh, stochastic conditions of arid Australia. The slow pace of life is further reflected in the age at which individuals attain a total length of 6.0 cm, which under captive rearing conditions at 26.571 °C [T = 26.571 °C] occurs approximately 326 days after the 120-day pre-birth period, giving a total of about 446 days from conception to the onset of reproductive potential. This protracted developmental timeline, spanning over a year from gamete fusion to the first opportunity for cloacal copulation, stands in contrast to many small, short-lived skink species that complete their life cycle within a single season.

Comparative analyses with other scincid lizards indicate that the Desert Skink exhibits a relatively high juvenile survivorship, likely linked to its burrowing habit and the attendant reduction in predation risk during the vulnerable yolk-sac larva and juvenile stages. The 1.85 g [Wwb = 1.85 g] wet weight at birth is roughly equivalent to the hatchling mass of several larger Egernia congeners, suggesting a tendency toward producing fewer, larger offspring. The transition from juvenile to sub-adult is marked by the achievement of 6.0 cm [Lp = 6.0 cm] total length and a body mass of approximately 7.63 g [Wwp = approximately 7.63 g], at which point gonadal activation commences. Interestingly, the length of the smallest female captured while gravid was 6.4 cm, slightly above the calculated 6.0 cm threshold, indicating that first reproduction may be deferred until a small additional size buffer is achieved. The ultimate length of 8.6 cm [Li = 8.6 cm] and the corresponding ultimate mass of around 21.41 g [Wwi = around 21.41 g] represent the terminal body dimensions, after which all available energy is directed toward annual gamete production and egg incubation.
